supportingMaterial.originalHTML:
Build a safe place to practice

Recommended Infrastructure Lab

Equivalent hardware and software are welcome. Physical hardware is not mandatory. Use legally obtained images and licenses, isolated networks and disposable test workloads.

01 / Beginner

Learn packet behavior

  • Cisco Packet Tracer
  • GNS3 or EVE-NG
  • Wireshark
  • Linux VM
  • Windows Server VM

Start with a small topology; capture traffic and keep a lab notebook.

02 / Intermediate

Operate an enterprise lab

  • Cisco IOSv / IOSvL2
  • CSR1000v / Catalyst 8000V
  • NX-OSv
  • FortiGate VM or equivalent firewall
  • Windows Server / Ubuntu Server
  • VMware ESXi or equivalent hypervisor

Check platform support and host resources before installing virtual appliances.

03 / Advanced physical

Test real dependencies

  • Catalyst 2960X / 9200
  • Cisco ISR4331
  • Nexus 3K / 5K / 9K
  • Access point + wireless controller
  • HPE DL380 Gen9 / Gen10
  • SAN storage + Brocade or Cisco SAN switch
  • UPS + managed PDU

Use equivalent platforms where practical; size power, memory and storage first.

Final project / design • validate • defend

Enterprise Data Center Architecture Capstone

Design an enterprise environment that can survive a failed link, device, power path or site. Explain every dependency, test your recovery assumptions, and make the design reproducible.

Your engineering deliverables

Career milestones are examples of skill progression. Job titles vary between organizations; completion is neither a job guarantee nor proof of production experience.

Logical reference only. EVPN controls a VXLAN overlay over the routed leaf-spine underlay. ACI is an alternative fabric operating model. Fibre Channel storage uses separate SAN paths from host HBAs; the storage attachment above represents workload dependency.

stages.title: IT & Infrastructure Foundation
stages.why: Physical components, operating systems and addressing determine what a network can carry and how it fails.
stages.lab: Build a small LAN with two PCs and a managed switch. Assign addresses, verify gateway reachability, and document the cable and port map.

stages.title: Networking Fundamentals
stages.why: Packet-level understanding lets you distinguish transport failures from application and addressing problems.
stages.lab: Capture ARP, DHCP, DNS, a TCP handshake and ICMP. Annotate packet fields, timings, and the path from client to gateway.

stages.title: Cisco Enterprise Networking
stages.why: Predictable Cisco configuration, resilient switching and recoverable boot processes underpin reliable enterprise operations.
stages.lab: Build three Cisco switches with redundant links. Configure VLANs, trunks, LACP EtherChannel, an STP root, PortFast and BPDU Guard. Test a link failure.

stages.title: Advanced Routing & Switching
stages.why: Routing policy, convergence and segmentation determine which path traffic takes during normal operation and failure.
stages.lab: Build two distribution switches and two routers. Configure HSRP, OSPF, BGP, VLAN segmentation and route filtering. Record convergence after a failure.

stages.title: Network Services
stages.why: Time, identity, naming and telemetry make infrastructure manageable, auditable and observable.
stages.lab: Centralize NTP, Syslog, SNMP and AAA. Verify timestamps, log delivery, polling, administrator authentication and a local recovery account.

stages.title: Network Security
stages.why: Explicit trust boundaries and verified controls reduce unauthorized access while preserving required business flows.
stages.lab: Design Internet, DMZ, Users, Servers, Management, Guest and Backup zones. Write explicit firewall and ACL rules; test allowed and denied flows.

stages.title: Data Center Foundations
stages.why: Power, cooling, server architecture and physical redundancy constrain every logical data center design.
stages.lab: Design a 3-rack data center. Produce rack elevations, dual power paths, cooling and cabling plans, a capacity worksheet and an out-of-band network.

stages.title: Cisco Data Center
stages.why: Fabric underlays, overlays and endpoint policy enable scalable east-west networking and resilient server attachment.
stages.lab: Model 2 spines and 4 leaves with servers, storage and firewalls. Explain VXLAN encapsulation, MP-BGP EVPN routes and vPC attachment; compare an ACI policy design.

stages.title: Storage & Virtualization
stages.why: Storage paths and hypervisor behavior determine workload availability, recovery and performance.
stages.lab: Design SAN storage, 2 SAN switches, 3 virtualization hosts, redundant network switches and shared storage. Validate path failover and VM recovery.

stages.title: Automation & Infrastructure Architecture
stages.why: Repeatable changes, documented intent and tested recovery turn individual configurations into an operable architecture.
stages.lab: Design and document the complete enterprise capstone. Use version-controlled automation, validation and rollback to reproduce the infrastructure.

OSPF.why: OSPF is a link-state interior routing protocol used to build resilient enterprise routed networks.
OSPF.lab: Build 4 routers with Area 0 and Area 10. Change interface cost, break an adjacency and compare the LSDB to the routing table.

BGP.why: BGP exchanges reachability using policy, allowing independent networks and EVPN fabrics to control route selection.
concepts: eBGP versus iBGP and next-hop reachability
AS Path, Local Preference and MED
BGP.lab: Connect two autonomous systems, advertise only approved prefixes and change Local Preference. Confirm path selection and failover.

VLAN.why: VLANs separate Layer 2 broadcast domains. Inter-VLAN traffic needs routing and an explicit policy.
VLAN.lab: Create user and server VLANs on two switches. Verify isolation, trunk carriage and gateway reachability.

RAID.why: RAID trades usable capacity, failure tolerance and performance. RAID does not replace independent backups.
RAID.lab: Model usable capacity and failures for each level. Use disposable virtual disks to test rebuild and recovery.

vPC.why: vPC lets a downstream device form a port channel to two Nexus peers while maintaining a loop-free attachment design.
vPC.lab: Model two peers and a dual-attached server. Test peer-link and keepalive failures separately and document forwarding behavior.

VXLAN.why: VXLAN encapsulates Layer 2 traffic over a routed IP underlay to scale logical segments beyond a single VLAN fabric.
VXLAN.lab: Build two VTEPs with a routed underlay. Verify a tenant segment and inspect encapsulation and MTU behavior.

Ansible.why: Ansible expresses repeatable tasks and desired configuration, reducing manual changes and configuration drift.
concepts: Idempotence, check mode and secrets handling
Ansible.lab: Back up three lab devices, render a reviewed configuration and apply a reversible change. Run it twice and inspect drift.

SAN.why: A SAN supplies block storage over dedicated or logically isolated paths. Availability depends on fabric and host path design.
SAN.lab: Diagram dual fabrics and host paths. Test a path failure using disposable workloads and confirm multipath state.

VMware ESXi.why: ESXi runs virtual workloads directly on a host; management, storage and workload networks need a coherent availability design.
VMware ESXi.lab: Use a supported evaluation or equivalent hypervisor to build a disposable host with separated management and storage networks.

Enterprise Data Center Architecture Caps.why: Bring all domains together in a defensible design that survives failures and can be operated, recovered and automated.
concepts: Dual ISPs and edge routers; HA firewalls
2 spines / 4 leaves, server farm and VMware cluster
Dual SAN fabrics, shared storage and independent backup
Management, AAA, DNS, DHCP, NTP, Syslog and monitoring
Automation server, NetBox, Ansible, Git and a DR site
Enterprise Data Center Architecture Caps.lab: Design and document the complete enterprise capstone. Use version-controlled automation, validation and rollback to reproduce the infrastructure.

CPU.why: CPU architecture sets compute capacity and workload compatibility. Frequency alone does not describe throughput.
CPU.lab: Inventory a lab host CPU and its virtualization capabilities. Compare a single-thread and multi-thread workload while observing utilization.

RAM.why: Memory capacity, speed and layout affect server stability and workload performance.
RAM.lab: Read a server memory inventory and its population guide. Diagram channels and diagnose memory pressure in a disposable VM.

Storage.why: Storage latency, throughput and durability constrain operating systems and application workloads.
Storage.lab: Attach a disposable virtual disk, partition it and mount a filesystem. Measure a small test workload and restore a deleted test file from backup.

PCIe.why: PCIe lanes and slot wiring constrain NIC, HBA and storage expansion bandwidth.
PCIe.lab: Draw the PCIe layout of a lab server from its platform guide; map each NIC and HBA to a slot and CPU.

NICs.why: A network interface joins a host to the network and exposes useful evidence of physical and link faults.
NICs.lab: Inventory a host NIC, observe counters, disconnect a lab cable and verify link state and recovery.

Windows.why: Windows client administration provides the endpoint perspective for enterprise network diagnosis.
Windows.lab: Use a lab client to inspect addressing, DNS resolution, routing and local firewall behavior.

Windows Server.why: Windows Server supplies common enterprise identity, addressing and naming services.
Windows Server.lab: Build an isolated evaluation VM. Install DNS and DHCP roles, validate a client lease and collect event logs.

Linux fundamentals.why: Linux underpins many infrastructure services, monitoring platforms and automation tools.
Linux fundamentals.lab: Build a Linux VM; manage a service, inspect routes and sockets, and troubleshoot a deliberately stopped service.

CLI fundamentals.why: CLI fluency makes investigation and repeated administrative tasks precise and reproducible.
CLI fundamentals.lab: Inspect addresses and routes, redirect output to a log, and explain each command and its result.

IPv4.why: IPv4 addressing identifies interfaces and defines local subnet boundaries used in forwarding decisions.
IPv4.lab: Assign two subnets to a small routed lab. Verify local versus routed traffic with packet captures.

IPv6.why: IPv6 adds a large address space and a distinct discovery model that infrastructure engineers must operate.
IPv6.lab: Build two dual-stack networks, inspect neighbor discovery and verify IPv6 gateway and DNS reachability.

CIDR.why: CIDR represents address blocks compactly and supports efficient allocation and summarization.
CIDR.lab: Allocate a /24 into differently sized subnets, check overlaps and explain the routing summary.

STP.why: Spanning Tree prevents Layer 2 loops while retaining redundant physical paths.
STP.lab: Build a three-switch triangle, select the root and fail an uplink. Confirm port-role changes and recovery using counters and captures.

LACP.why: LACP negotiates link aggregation so multiple compatible links can behave as one logical interface.
LACP.lab: Bundle two lab links, verify the channel and remove one member. Test traffic and document why one flow does not use the aggregate bandwidth.

DNS.why: DNS translates names into service endpoints; naming failures often resemble connectivity failures.
concepts: A, AAAA, CNAME and PTR records
DNS.lab: Build a local zone, query it with dig or nslookup and compare a missing record with an unreachable resolver.

DHCP.why: DHCP gives clients addressing information and service options through a stateful lease process.
DHCP.lab: Capture a full lease exchange. Exhaust a small test scope, diagnose the failure and restore lease availability.

NAT / PAT.why: Address translation maps address realms and conserves public addresses through port translation.
NAT / PAT.lab: Configure translation in an isolated routed lab. Inspect mappings and test an intentionally missing return route.

SNMP.why: SNMP exposes device metrics and events for operational monitoring.
SNMP.lab: Use SNMPv3 to read lab interface counters. Generate a link event and validate monitoring timestamps.

IP SLA.why: IP SLA actively measures service reachability or performance and can feed object tracking.
IP SLA.lab: Configure a lab reachability probe and tracked route. Fail the path, measure detection time and verify recovery.

DHCP Snooping.why: DHCP snooping builds a client binding table and blocks untrusted DHCP server messages.
concepts: Dependencies of DAI and IP Source Guard
DHCP Snooping.lab: Introduce a rogue DHCP server in a lab VLAN, verify it is blocked and inspect the legitimate bindings.

IPsec.why: IPsec secures IP traffic using authenticated security associations and encryption where configured.
IPsec.lab: Build a lab site-to-site VPN. Check negotiation, verify protected traffic and diagnose mismatched selectors.

Firewall fundamentals.why: A firewall enforces policy between security boundaries using traffic context and, commonly, connection state.
concepts: Logging, rule order and change validation
Firewall fundamentals.lab: Build users, servers and DMZ zones. Permit required flows, test denied flows and save the matching policy logs.

EVPN.why: EVPN distributes endpoint and reachability information using BGP for overlay fabrics.
EVPN.lab: Use a two-leaf fabric to inspect MAC/IP advertisements and demonstrate tenant isolation and a withdrawn route.

vMotion.why: vMotion moves a running VM between hosts and depends on compatible compute, storage and network paths.
vMotion.lab: Migrate a disposable VM between compatible lab hosts while observing workload reachability and migration traffic.

Snapshots.why: Snapshots record a point-in-time disk state for short-term rollback and have operational limits.
Snapshots.lab: Take a snapshot of a disposable VM, change a test file, revert and consolidate. Document why independent backups are still required.

Python Fundamentals.why: Python helps turn repeated investigation and configuration tasks into clear, testable programs.
Python Fundamentals.lab: Read a local device inventory, validate IP addresses and generate a structured report with explicit error handling.

NETCONF.why: NETCONF exchanges structured configuration and operational data using a model-aware protocol.
NETCONF.lab: Query capabilities on a supported lab device, retrieve configuration and test a reversible edit with validation.

RESTCONF.why: RESTCONF provides HTTP access to YANG-modeled configuration and operational data.
RESTCONF.lab: Read a modeled interface from a supported lab device, apply a reversible change and verify the response and resulting state.

Git.why: Git records configuration and automation changes with reviewable history.
Git.lab: Commit a sanitized lab configuration and playbook, review a branch change and restore an earlier version.

NetBox.why: NetBox can act as a source of truth for inventory, addressing and desired infrastructure intent.
NetBox.lab: Model a small lab inventory and address plan. Read the API and render configuration from reviewed intent.

RTO.why: Recovery Time Objective is the target time to restore a service after disruption.
RTO.lab: Time a disposable service recovery, include dependencies and compare the measured result to the documented target.

RPO.why: Recovery Point Objective describes the acceptable data-loss window after a disruption.
RPO.lab: Restore disposable application data from backup and quantify the missing interval against the target RPO.
